title: NVMePass: A Lightweight, High-performance and Scalable NVMe Virtualization Architecture with I/O Queues Passthrough
problem: Existing NVMe virtualization approaches either suffer severe performance degradation (Virtio software path) or require dedicated hardware with limited VM scalability (VFIO/SR-IOV hardware passthrough). No solution simultaneously achieves near-native I/O performance, zero CPU overhead, and high VM count scalability.
motivation: Cloud storage workloads demand low-latency NVMe access at scale; performance and CPU overhead trade-offs in existing virtualization approaches constrain cloud providers' ability to consolidate VMs without SLA degradation.
method: NVMePass allows virtual machines to communicate directly with NVMe storage devices, bypassing the hypervisor (the software layer that normally mediates all access). Each VM is assigned exclusive I/O queues (communication channels with the storage) and storage space (logical block address ranges) that cannot overlap. A new hardware component called an NVMe Resource Domain (NRD), built into the storage controller itself, acts as a security guard for storage access—it checks every request and blocks any VM from accessing storage assigned to another VM. Because the hypervisor no longer needs to inspect every storage operation, the system achieves near-native performance without the slowdown that comes from software mediation.
key_novelty: The key innovation is a hardware component (NVMe Resource Domain) embedded in the storage controller that enforces VM isolation and enables full I/O queue passthrough without any hypervisor involvement in the storage data path.
contributions: NVMePass architecture enabling NVMe I/O queue passthrough to VMs with zero hypervisor involvement in the data path.
NVMe Resource Domain (NRD) hardware primitive for device-level VM isolation and illegal I/O request interception.
DMA and interrupt remapping mechanism eliminating virtualization overhead without dedicated SR-IOV hardware.
100.1-100.5% IOPS of VFIO at comparable performance; 40% lower latency vs. SPDK-Vhost at 150 VMs; 68% throughput improvement in real-world apps at 100 VMs.

metrics.speedup: 40% lower latency vs. SPDK-Vhost at 150 VMs; 68% IOPS improvement vs. SPDK-Vhost in real-world app at 100 VMs

limitations: NRD requires modifications to the NVMe controller hardware, necessitating vendor cooperation and may not be compatible with commodity off-the-shelf NVMe drives.
primary_theme: Hardware-assisted NVMe I/O queue passthrough virtualization with in-device VM isolation
